title: What Is CBN (Cannabinol)? Effects and the Sleep Question
h1: CBN, Explained: How It Forms and What the Research Shows
metaDescription: What is CBN? How cannabinol forms as THC ages, how it compares with CBD, what sleep research really shows, how long it lingers and where it stands legally.
excerpt: CBN forms as THC breaks down with age. Here's how it acts in the body, what sleep research does and doesn't show, and what to know about the law and drug tests.
keyTakeaways: CBN forms when THC breaks down through air oxidation, so older, poorly stored cannabis tends to hold more of it.
It binds CB1, the receptor behind THC's high, with about a tenth of THC's affinity, so on its own its effects are mild at most.
Sleep claims outrun the evidence: in a 2026 trial, even very high doses did not change the main sleep measure.
CBN can trip some THC urine screens at high enough levels, so CBN products aren't a way around a drug test.
body:
What is CBN? Cannabinol, or CBN, is a cannabinoid that forms as THC breaks down over time. You'll often see it in evening-themed gummies and tinctures, but the science behind its sleepy reputation is thin. Here's how CBN forms, how it compares with CBD, what studies actually found, and what to know about drug tests and the law.

## What is CBN? A breakdown product of aging THC

Unlike THC and CBD, CBN isn't built by the plant's enzymes; no biosynthetic pathway for it has been identified. Instead, it forms when THC reacts with oxygen in the air and slowly changes structure. Small amounts of its acid form, CBNA, turn up in some hemp, which suggests THCA can oxidize too.

So CBN doesn't come from heating THCA, the way THC does; it comes from aging. Cannabis in careless storage gradually loses THC and gains CBN. CBN was also the first cannabinoid ever isolated, in the late 1800s, from hashish that had often spent months in transit to European labs. Our guide to [storing cannabis](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) explains how to slow the process.

## How CBN interacts with CB1 and CB2

CBN binds both main cannabinoid receptors, but not the way THC does. Its affinity for CB1, the receptor behind THC's high, is about ten times lower than THC's, and it's less effective at switching that receptor on. At CB2, a receptor linked to immune signaling, results disagree: older work rated CBN about as potent as THC, while more recent work found it two to four times weaker.

In plain terms, CBN reaches for the same switch as THC with a much weaker grip, which helps explain why it produces little on its own.

## CBN compared with CBD

| | CBN | CBD |
|---|---|---|
| Where it comes from | THC breaking down with age and air | Made by the plant, from CBDA |
| Activity at CB1 | Weak, about a tenth of THC's affinity | Doesn't produce a high |
| Intoxicating? | Mild at most, mainly alongside THC | No |
| Research base | Small, mostly older studies plus a few recent trials | Much larger, including human trials |

CBD is a major product of the plant itself, while CBN is a byproduct of time. Our overview of [cannabinoids](/blog/what-are-cannabinoids/) shows where each fits, and our guides to [CBG](/blog/what-is-cbg-cannabigerol/) and [CBC](/blog/what-is-cbc-cannabichromene/) cover two more minor cannabinoids.

## The sleep question: what studies show

CBN's sleepy reputation is tied to old flower, and products market it for evenings. The research hasn't kept up. A 2022 review put the marketed doses at generally under 5 mg a day and concluded that, from a clinical standpoint, CBN's sleep-inducing reputation is unsubstantiated.

A more rigorous test came in 2026. Researchers in Sydney gave 20 adults with diagnosed insomnia a single 30 mg or 300 mg dose of CBN, or a placebo, then measured their sleep in a lab. Neither dose significantly changed the study's main measure: time spent awake after first falling asleep. The 300 mg dose, more than 60 times the marketed doses that review described, did shift some secondary measures, such as how quickly people fell asleep and how they rated their sleep. The trial recorded 247 mild to moderate adverse events across its two doses and placebo, and the authors called for larger, longer trials.

That's one night, 20 people and a very high dose, so it's far from proof. If sleep is a regular struggle, talk with a clinician; ongoing sleep problems can have causes worth looking into.

## CBN and intoxication: mild at most

On its own, CBN doesn't seem to do much. In a small 1970s study of five men, 50 mg of CBN alone didn't change pain thresholds or skin sensitivity. Pairing it with THC modestly increased drowsiness and dizziness compared with THC alone.

So if a CBN product also contains THC, the THC will shape most of what you feel. Check the milligrams of each, start low and give it time.

## Where CBN appears: gummies, tinctures, vapes and aged flower

- **Gummies and tinctures** marketed for evenings, sometimes combined with THC, CBD or both
- **Vapes** that list CBN among their cannabinoids
- **Aged flower**, where THC has had time to oxidize

Fresh, well-stored flower usually holds little CBN, and only the label or lab report can tell you how much a product contains.

## Legal status in Michigan and federally

Michigan draws its line by THC content. Cannabis above 0.3% THC, THCA included, counts as marijuana, and only licensed marijuana businesses may sell it, so CBN products made from it are sold in licensed stores. Only adults 21 and older can buy for adult use, while registered medical patients 18 and older can buy with a valid card.

Federal hemp law is changing. Congress has narrowed the definition of hemp to count total THC, including THCA. It also excludes finished products with more than 0.4 mg per container of THC and other cannabinoids with similar effects, as federal health officials determine them. As of October 2026, the change is set to take effect in late 2026, and further changes are possible, so be cautious about online claims for hemp-derived CBN. Our [Michigan cannabis law guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/) covers the state's other rules.

## CBN half-life and detection

Few studies have measured how long CBN lingers, and they're decades old. A half-life is the time it takes blood levels to fall by half. In a 1987 study of six men, CBN's average half-life was about 32 hours after an intravenous dose and 43 hours after smoking, with wide variation.

Drug testing is the bigger practical issue. In a 2020 lab study, CBN cross-reacted with two common urine tests designed to detect THC's breakdown product. At roughly 5 to 20 times the THC level each test is set to catch, CBN alone produced a positive screen, and on one of the tests it added to the signal from THC. Some CBN products contain THC too, so if you're drug tested, assume a CBN product could cause a positive result.

faq.q: What does research actually say about CBN and sleep?
faq.a: Not much, yet. A 2022 review called CBN's sleep-inducing reputation unsubstantiated, and older human studies were small. In a 2026 trial of 20 adults with insomnia, single doses of 30 or 300 mg didn't change the study's main measure of nighttime waking, though the high dose shifted some secondary measures. The same review put typical marketed doses at under 5 mg a day. Talk with a clinician about ongoing sleep problems.

faq.q: Can CBN cause a high on its own?
faq.a: Not much of one, if any. CBN binds CB1, the receptor behind THC's high, with about a tenth of THC's affinity. In a small 1970s study, 50 mg of CBN alone did little, while combining it with THC modestly increased drowsiness and dizziness. If a CBN product also contains THC, expect the THC to set the tone.

Yes. As cannabis ages, THC slowly reacts with oxygen and turns into CBN, especially with air exposure and careless storage. Old flower can carry noticeably more CBN and less THC than it did when fresh. That doesn't make stale flower a sleep aid; it mostly means weaker THC effects. Keep cannabis airtight and somewhere cool and dark to slow the change.

faq.q: How long can CBN be detected?
faq.a: There's little direct research. A 1987 study of six men put CBN's average half-life at about 32 to 43 hours, with wide variation. For drug tests, the bigger concern is that CBN can trip some THC urine screens at high enough levels, and some CBN products contain THC as well. If you're tested, assume a CBN product could cause a positive result.

review.summary: 26 claims checked: 21 ok, 5 fixed (3 overstated, 2 unsupported). All six sources reopened (abstracts, the Maioli full text, the statute text) and support the text as edited.

claims.claim: CBN forms when THC breaks down through air oxidation; no biosynthetic pathway has been identified; older, poorly stored cannabis holds more of it (takeaway 1, section 1, FAQ 3)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/ (full text via Europe PMC): "a biosynthetic pathway for cannabinolic acid (CBNA ...), and so of CBN ... itself, has not been identified; the latter is a degradation artifact of Δ9-THC which, as result of air oxidation, undergoes aromatization"

claims.claim: Small amounts of CBNA turn up in some hemp, suggesting THCA can oxidize too
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/: "small amounts of CBNA have been found in some hemp samples, suggesting that, in particular conditions, oxidative degradation may also occur to tetrahydrocannabinolic acid"

claims.claim: CBN does not come from heating THCA the way THC does (it is not a decarboxylation product); it comes from aging
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/ (oxidative degradation product of THC); brief: CBN forms as THC oxidizes, not by decarboxylation

claims.claim: CBN was the first cannabinoid isolated, in the late 1800s, from hashish that often spent months in transit to European labs
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/: "it was the first phytocannabinoid to be isolated from hashish in the late 19th century"; "the long journey between the collection site and the European laboratories, usually lasting months, combined with uncontrolled and careless storage conditions"

claims.claim: CBN's CB1 affinity is about ten times lower than THC's and it is less effective at switching CB1 on (takeaway 2, section 2, table, FAQ 2)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/: "The affinity of CBN for the CB1 receptors are 10 times lower when compared to that of Δ9-THC"; "CBN is less effective than Δ9-THC at inhibiting the CB1 receptor-mediated activity of adenylyl cyclase"

claims.claim: At CB2, older work rated CBN about as potent as THC; more recent work found it two to four times weaker
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/: "previously CBN was considered an agonist with the same potency as Δ9-THC, it has recently been reported to have a potency between 2–4 times lower"

claims.claim: Products market CBN for evenings "typically at doses under 5 mg a day"; FAQ 1 "Typical products contain under 5 mg"; the 300 mg dose is "roughly 60 times what a typical product contains"
claims.fix: the under-5 mg figure is a 2021 observation (Corroon 2021, cited by the 2022 review) stated as today's typical product; now attributed: "A 2022 review put the marketed doses at generally under 5 mg a day", "more than 60 times the marketed doses that review described", FAQ "The same review put typical marketed doses at under 5 mg a day"
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/: marketed as "the sleepy cannabinoid in old weed" at dosages generally less than 5 mg/die [81]; reference 81 = Corroon J, Cannabis Cannabinoid Res 2021

claims.claim: A 2022 review concluded CBN's sleep-inducing reputation is clinically unsubstantiated (body, FAQ 1)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/: "It is therefore unsubstantiated that CBN has sleep-inducing properties, from a clinical perspective"

claims.claim: "The strongest test so far came in 2026"
claims.fix: an unsupported superlative; now "A more rigorous test came in 2026"
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13357646/ (abstract via Europe PMC): describes itself as testing effects on objective sleep and insomnia that "remain unknown"; it does not rank itself against other trials

claims.claim: 2026 trial: researchers in Sydney gave 20 adults with diagnosed insomnia a single 30 mg or 300 mg dose or placebo and measured sleep in a lab; neither dose significantly changed wake after sleep onset, the main measure (takeaway 3, FAQ 1)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13357646/ (abstract, PMID 41698831): "Twenty adults ... with physician-diagnosed insomnia disorder" at the Woolcock Institute, Sydney; "a single 2 mL oral dose of 30 mg ... or 300 mg ... cannabinol, or matched placebo"; "Cannabinol did not significantly change WASO"

claims.claim: The 300 mg dose shifted secondary measures such as sleep onset and rated sleep quality
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13357646/: "300 mg cannabinol increased non-rapid eye movement-2 sleep ..., subjective sleep quality ...; and reduced sleep onset latency"

claims.claim: "Mild to moderate side effects showed up in all three conditions, placebo included"
claims.fix: the abstract gives only a total across arms (the full text was not reachable: Wiley 403, no results on ClinicalTrials.gov); now "The trial recorded 247 mild to moderate adverse events across its two doses and placebo"
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13357646/: "There were 247 mild-to-moderate adverse events across arms."

claims.claim: The authors called for larger trials
claims.fix: none (now "larger, longer trials", the abstract's words)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13357646/: "Larger, longer trials are warranted."

claims.claim: In a small 1970s study of five men, 50 mg of CBN alone did not change pain thresholds or skin sensitivity; with THC it modestly increased drowsiness and dizziness (body, FAQ 2)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9658060/: "a small clinical trial involving five male volunteers who received oral CBN (50 mg)"; "pain threshold and skin sensitivity, which are not affected by CBN alone"; "modest increases in some subjective outcomes (drowsiness and dizziness)"; references are Takahashi and Karniol 1975 and Karniol et al. 1975

claims.claim: If a CBN product also contains THC, the THC shapes most of the effect; check milligrams, start low

review.notes: Independent fact-check, 2026-10-24. Maioli 2022 read in full (Europe PMC XML), including its reference list to date the under-5 mg figure (Corroon 2021) and the five-volunteer study (1975). Lavender 2026: abstract only (no PMC body via Europe PMC or E-utilities, Wiley 403, no posted results on ClinicalTrials.gov), so its adverse-event sentence now repeats the abstract. Johansson 1987 and Kroner 2020 abstracts read through NCBI E-utilities; P.L. 119-37 sec. 781 read on govinfo. High Society is no longer named in this medical article. Writer's notes: Medical brief: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links; no where-to-buy FAQ. CBN described as forming by oxidation, not decarboxylation. No claim that CBN avoids drug tests.
